title: Find one user among 10 million
body: A login looks up a user by email: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'an@example.com'`. The `users` table has 10 million rows and no index on `email`, so the database must check every row: a **full table scan**. Even with the table in memory this takes hundreds of milliseconds; from disk it can take seconds.

title: How many pages does the index read?
body: The team adds an **index** on `email`: a B-tree whose nodes each hold hundreds of sorted keys. A lookup starts at the root and picks one branch per level. With about 300 keys per node, three levels already cover 300 × 300 × 300 = 27 million entries, so the lookup reads about 3 or 4 pages and then the one row. It takes about 1 ms instead of a second.

predict.question: A B-tree index on email covers 10 million rows, and each index node holds about 300 keys. About how many index pages does one lookup read?
options: Exactly 1, because indexes are hash maps
predict.explanation: Each level of the tree chooses among about 300 branches: 300, then 90,000, then 27 million entries. Three or four levels cover 10 million rows. A binary search needs about 23 steps because it chooses between only two at each step; B-tree nodes are much wider.

title: Every index costs something on writes
body: Indexes are not free. When a new user signs up, the database writes the row and also adds an entry to every index on the table. With indexes on `id` (the primary key) and `email`, one insert does three pieces of work. Indexes also take storage. Add an index for queries that run often on a large table, not for every column.

title: A transaction: all or nothing
body: Moving 50 dollars from account A to account B needs two updates. If the server crashes after the first, money vanishes. A **transaction** groups them: `BEGIN; UPDATE … A − 50; UPDATE … B + 50; COMMIT;`. Either both changes are saved or neither is (**atomicity**), and once committed they survive a crash (**durability**).

title: Two buyers, one seat
body: One seat is left. Buyer A's request reads `seats_left = 1`. Before it writes, Buyer B's request also reads `seats_left = 1`. Both then write `seats_left = 0` and both confirm a ticket. Each step looked correct on its own, but the check and the write were separate, so the second buyer slipped in between: a **race condition**.

predict.question: Both requests read seats_left = 1, then both write seats_left = 0 and confirm a ticket. How many tickets were sold for the last seat?
options: 1, because the database queues the requests
predict.explanation: Each request checked first and wrote later, in separate steps. Both checks saw 1 before either write happened, so both confirmed a ticket. Writing 0 twice gives the same row value, which hides the problem: two people paid for one seat.

title: Put the check inside the write
body: The fix is a **conditional update**: `UPDATE concerts SET seats_left = seats_left - 1 WHERE id = 42 AND seats_left > 0`. The database applies the two updates one after the other on the row, and the second one re-checks the condition on the new value. Buyer A's update changes 1 row; Buyer B's update finds `seats_left = 0` and changes 0 rows, so B is told the seat is gone. A **unique constraint** on the seat number gives the same protection when each sale is a new row.

title: Lock first, or check a version
body: When a change needs more than one statement, two general approaches exist. **Pessimistic**: inside one transaction, `BEGIN`, read the row with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` (this locks it), check `seats_left > 0`, decrement it, then `COMMIT`. The lock is held until the commit, so Buyer B's locking read waits, then sees 0 and gets "sold out". A locking read on its own, outside a transaction, releases the lock at once and protects nothing. It suits rows that many users fight over. **Optimistic**: read the row without a lock, say with `version = 7`, check `seats_left > 0`, then write `SET seats_left = seats_left - 1, version = 8 WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7`. Changing the version in the same update is what stops a second buyer who also read 7. If 0 rows update, someone changed the row first: read it again and retry, or report a conflict. Every write to the row must change the version. It suits rows that are rarely changed at the same time. In both cases, confirm the sale only after the commit.
